Page: API Reference


Viabl can render a beautiful, interactive API reference directly from your OpenAPI specification. Point to your spec file in page frontmatter and Viabl handles the rest — endpoints, parameters, request and response schemas, and authentication are all rendered automatically.

## Quick start

Place your OpenAPI spec at the root of your docs project:

```
my-docs/
├── docs.json
├── introduction.mdx
└── openapi.yaml       ← your spec file
```

Create an MDX page and point to it using the `openapi` frontmatter field:

```mdx
---
title: API Reference
openapi: /openapi.yaml
---
```

Register the page in your `docs.json` navigation:

```json
"navigation": [
  {
    "group": "Getting Started",
    "pages": ["introduction"]
  },
  {
    "group": "API Reference",
    "pages": ["api-reference"]
  }
]
```

That is all. Viabl reads your spec and renders the full API reference on that page.

## Supported formats

Both YAML and JSON spec files are supported:

```mdx
---
title: API Reference
openapi: /openapi.yaml
---
```

```mdx
---
title: API Reference
openapi: /openapi.json
---
```

Place the file anywhere in your project root and reference it with an absolute path from the root.

## Filtering by tag

For large APIs it is cleaner to split the reference into multiple pages — one per tag. Use the `openapiTag` frontmatter field to filter the spec to a specific tag:

```mdx
---
title: Users
openapi: /openapi.yaml
openapiTag: Users
---
```

```mdx
---
title: Projects
openapi: /openapi.yaml
openapiTag: Projects
---
```

Each page renders only the endpoints matching that tag. Register them individually in your navigation:

```json
{
  "group": "API Reference",
  "pages": [
    "api-reference/overview",
    "api-reference/users",
    "api-reference/projects",
    "api-reference/billing"
  ]
}
```

<Tip>
  Tag your endpoints in the spec itself using the `tags` field on each operation. The `openapiTag` value must match the tag name exactly.
</Tip>

## Frontmatter fields

<ResponseField name="openapi" type="string">
  Path to your OpenAPI spec file relative to the project root. Supports both `.yaml` and `.json` formats.

```mdx
---

title: API Reference
openapi: /openapi.yaml

---
```

</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="openapiTag" type="string">
  Filter the spec to only show endpoints matching this tag. The value must match a tag name defined in your spec exactly — it is case sensitive.

```mdx
---

title: Users API
openapi: /openapi.yaml
openapiTag: Users

---
```

</ResponseField>

<Warning>
  When `openapi` is set in frontmatter, any MDX content below the frontmatter block is ignored. The entire page body is replaced by the rendered API reference.
</Warning>

pageContent:
## Example spec structure

A minimal OpenAPI spec that works well with Viabl:

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3

info:
  title: My API
  description: API documentation for My Product
  version: 1.0.0

servers:
  - url: https://api.example.com/v1
    description: Production

tags:
  - name: Users
    description: User management endpoints
  - name: Projects
    description: Project management endpoints

paths:
  /users:
    get:
      tags: [Users]
      summary: List users
      description: Returns a paginated list of all users.
      parameters:
        - name: page
          in: query
          schema:
            type: integer
            default: 1
        - name: limit
          in: query
          schema:
            type: integer
            default: 20
      responses:
        "200":
          description: A list of users
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: object
                properties:
                  data:
                    type: array
                    items:
                      $ref: "#/components/schemas/User"
                  total:
                    type: integer

  /users/{id}:
    get:
      tags: [Users]
      summary: Get a user
      parameters:
        - name: id
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The user
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/User"
        "404":
          description: User not found

components:
  schemas:
    User:
      type: object
      properties:
        id:
          type: string
          example: usr_01abc123
        email:
          type: string
          format: email
          example: jane@example.com
        name:
          type: string
          example: Jane Smith
        createdAt:
          type: string
          format: date-time

  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth:
      type: http
      scheme: bearer
      bearerFormat: JWT

security:
  - bearerAuth: []
```

## Mixing API and prose pages

You can mix OpenAPI pages with regular MDX pages in the same navigation group. A common pattern is to have an overview page followed by the API reference:

```json
{
  "group": "API Reference",
  "pages": [
    "api-reference/overview",
    "api-reference/authentication",
    "api-reference/errors",
    "api-reference/users",
    "api-reference/projects"
  ]
}
```

Where `overview.mdx`, `authentication.mdx`, and `errors.mdx` are regular MDX pages covering concepts, and `users.mdx` and `projects.mdx` are OpenAPI pages using the `openapi` frontmatter field.

pageContent:
## Authentication

Define authentication schemes in your spec using `securitySchemes` and Viabl renders them automatically in the API reference:

```yaml
components:
  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth:
      type: http
      scheme: bearer
      bearerFormat: JWT
    apiKey:
      type: apiKey
      in: header
      name: X-API-Key

security:
  - bearerAuth: []
```

You can also apply security schemes per endpoint to override the global setting:

```yaml
paths:
  /public/status:
    get:
      summary: Health check
      security: [] # ← no auth required for this endpoint
```

## Multiple spec files

You can use different spec files on different pages — useful when you have multiple APIs or versioned specs:

```mdx
---
title: v1 API Reference
openapi: /openapi-v1.yaml
---
```

```mdx
---
title: v2 API Reference
openapi: /openapi-v2.yaml
---
```

Both files should be placed at the project root.

## What gets rendered

Viabl renders the following from your OpenAPI spec:

<Check>All endpoints grouped by tag</Check>
<Check>HTTP method and path for each endpoint</Check>
<Check>Summary and description</Check>
<Check>Path, query, header, and cookie parameters</Check>
<Check>Request body schema with field types and descriptions</Check>
<Check>Response schemas for all status codes</Check>
<Check>Authentication requirements</Check>
<Check>Example values from the spec</Check>

Page: Accordion


## Overview

The `Accordion` and `AccordionGroup` components let you hide and reveal content on demand. They are ideal for FAQs, optional details, and progressive disclosure of complex information.

- **Accordion**: A single collapsible section with a title and toggle.
- **AccordionGroup**: A wrapper for grouping multiple accordions together.

---

## Example

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is Docsmith?">
    Docsmith is a documentation framework built on Next.js that lets you write
    docs in MDX.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="How do I add a new page?">
    Create a new `.mdx` file in your `docs` folder and it will automatically
    appear in the sidebar.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Is it open source?" defaultOpen>
    Yes — Docsmith is fully open source and available on GitHub.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

---

## Usage

### Basic accordion

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <Accordion title="What is this?">
      This is the content inside the accordion.
    </Accordion>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Accordion title="What is this?">
      This is the content inside the accordion.
    </Accordion>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Open by default

Use `defaultOpen` to have an accordion expanded on initial render:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <Accordion title="Already open" defaultOpen>
      This accordion starts expanded.
    </Accordion>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Accordion title="Already open" defaultOpen>
      This accordion starts expanded.
    </Accordion>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Grouped accordions

Wrap multiple `Accordion` components in `AccordionGroup` for consistent spacing:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <AccordionGroup>
      <Accordion title="First question">
        Answer to the first question.
      </Accordion>
      <Accordion title="Second question">
        Answer to the second question.
      </Accordion>
      <Accordion title="Third question">
        Answer to the third question.
      </Accordion>
    </AccordionGroup>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <AccordionGroup>
      <Accordion title="First question">
        Answer to the first question.
      </Accordion>
      <Accordion title="Second question">
        Answer to the second question.
      </Accordion>
      <Accordion title="Third question">
        Answer to the third question.
      </Accordion>
    </AccordionGroup>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Accordion with rich content

Accordion content supports any valid MDX including code blocks and other components:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
        <Accordion title="How do I install the package?">
            Run the following command
            ```bash
                npm install my-package
            ```

                Then import it in your project:

            ```ts
            import { something } from "my-package";
            ```
        </Accordion>
    `````

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
 
        <Accordion title="How do I install the package?">
            Run the following command
            ```bash
                npm install my-package
            ```

                Then import it in your project:

            ```ts
            import { something } from "my-package";
            ```
        </Accordion>

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Props

**Accordion**

| Prop          | Type              | Required | Default | Description                                          |
| ------------- | ----------------- | -------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`       | `string`          | Yes      | —       | The heading shown in the clickable toggle bar.       |
| `children`    | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | —       | Content revealed when the accordion is expanded.     |
| `defaultOpen` | `boolean`         | No       | `false` | Whether the accordion is expanded on initial render. |

**AccordionGroup**

| Prop       | Type              | Required | Description                                           |
| ---------- | ----------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | One or more `Accordion` components to group together. |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- The toggle is a `<button>` element and is fully keyboard accessible.
- Use clear, descriptive titles so users can anticipate the content before expanding.
- Avoid nesting accordions inside other accordions as this creates confusing hierarchy.

metadata.title: Accordion
metadata.description: Collapsible content sections for organizing information without overwhelming the reader.

Page: Badge


## Overview

The `Badge` component renders a compact inline label with a colored background. It is ideal for tagging content with status indicators, version labels, or categorical metadata inline with text.

---

## Example

<Badge>Default</Badge> <Badge variant="success">Success</Badge>
<Badge variant="warning">Warning</Badge> <Badge variant="error">Error</Badge>
<Badge variant="info">Info</Badge>

---

## Usage

### Variants

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
```mdx
    <Badge>Default</Badge>

    <Badge variant="success">Success</Badge>

    <Badge variant="warning">Warning</Badge>

    <Badge variant="error">Error</Badge>

    <Badge variant="info">Info</Badge>

````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Badge>Default</Badge>

    <Badge variant="success">Success</Badge>

    <Badge variant="warning">Warning</Badge>

    <Badge variant="error">Error</Badge>

    <Badge variant="info">Info</Badge>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Inline with text

Badges are inline elements and sit naturally within prose:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
```mdx
    This feature is <Badge variant="success">stable</Badge> and ready for production.

    The `/v1/legacy` endpoint is <Badge variant="warning">deprecated</Badge> and will be removed in v3.

    This method is <Badge variant="error">removed</Badge> as of version 2.0.
````

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    This feature is <Badge variant="success">stable</Badge> and ready for production.

    The `/v1/legacy` endpoint is <Badge variant="warning">deprecated</Badge> and will be removed in v3.

    This method is <Badge variant="error">removed</Badge> as of version 2.0.

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Props

| Prop       | Type                                                   | Required | Default     | Description                                     |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | -------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode`                                      | Yes      | —           | The text or content displayed inside the badge. |
| `variant`  | `"default"` `"success"` `"warning"` `"error"` `"info"` | No       | `"default"` | Controls the color scheme of the badge.         |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- Badges are rendered as `<span>` elements and are inline by nature.
- Do not rely solely on color to convey meaning — always use descriptive text inside the badge.
- Avoid using badges as interactive elements; they are purely presentational.

metadata.title: Badge
metadata.description: Small inline labels for conveying status, categories, or metadata at a glance.

Page: Callout


## Overview

The `Callout` component draws attention to important information using colored banners with icons. Four semantic variants are available, each with a distinct color and icon to convey meaning at a glance.

It is also available via four shorthand aliases: `Note`, `Warning`, `Tip`, and `Danger`.

---

## Example

<Callout type="info">This is an informational callout.</Callout>

<Callout type="warn">This is a warning callout.</Callout>

<Callout type="error">This is an error callout.</Callout>

<Callout type="success">This is a success callout.</Callout>

---

## Usage

### Default (info)

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <Callout>This is an informational callout.</Callout>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Callout>This is an informational callout.</Callout>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Variants

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
```mdx
    <Callout type="info">Informational message.</Callout>

    <Callout type="warn">Something might go wrong.</Callout>

    <Callout type="error">Something went wrong.</Callout>

    <Callout type="success">Everything looks good.</Callout>

````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Callout type="info">Informational message.</Callout>

    <Callout type="warn">Something might go wrong.</Callout>

    <Callout type="error">Something went wrong.</Callout>

    <Callout type="success">Everything looks good.</Callout>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Shorthand aliases

For convenience, four aliases map directly to callout variants:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
```mdx
    <Note>This uses the info variant.</Note>

    <Warning>This uses the warn variant.</Warning>

    <Danger>This uses the error variant.</Danger>

    <Tip>This uses the success variant.</Tip>
````

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Note>This uses the info variant.</Note>

    <Warning>This uses the warn variant.</Warning>

    <Danger>This uses the error variant.</Danger>

    <Tip>This uses the success variant.</Tip>

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Callout with rich content

Callouts support any inline MDX content:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <Note>
      Make sure to set your `API_KEY` environment variable before running the
      server. See the [configuration guide](/configuration) for details.
    </Note>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Note>
      Make sure to set your `API_KEY` environment variable before running the
      server. See the [configuration guide](/configuration) for details.
    </Note>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Props

**Callout**

| Prop       | Type                                    | Required | Default  | Description                                        |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `type`     | `"info"` `"warn"` `"error"` `"success"` | No       | `"info"` | Controls the color scheme and icon of the callout. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode`                       | Yes      | —        | The content displayed inside the callout.          |

**Shorthand aliases**

| Component   | Equivalent                 |
| ----------- | -------------------------- |
| `<Note>`    | `<Callout type="info">`    |
| `<Warning>` | `<Callout type="warn">`    |
| `<Tip>`     | `<Callout type="success">` |
| `<Danger>`  | `<Callout type="error">`   |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- Callouts are rendered as `<div>` elements with no ARIA role by default. For critical alerts, consider adding `role="alert"` to the component.
- Do not rely solely on color to convey meaning — the icon and content together provide sufficient context.
- Avoid overusing callouts on a single page as they lose impact when too frequent.

metadata.title: Callout
metadata.description: Highlight important information with contextual callout banners.

Page: Cards


## Overview

The `Card` and `CardGroup` components provide a flexible way to present content in a clean, grid-based layout. They are ideal for navigation, feature highlights, and documentation entry points.

- **Card**: A single content container with optional icon and link.
- **CardGroup**: A responsive grid wrapper for organizing multiple cards.

---

## Example

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Getting Started" icon="Rocket" href="/introduction">
    Get up and running quickly.
  </Card>
  <Card title="API Reference" icon="Code2" href="/api-reference/overview">
    Explore all available endpoints.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

---

## Card

A responsive grid layout for organizing multiple Card components.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <Card title="Getting Started">Get up and running quickly.</Card>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Card title="Getting Started">Get up and running quickly.</Card>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

**Icon Usage**

Icons are resolved dynamically from lucide-react. If the icon name is not found, the value will be rendered as plain text or emoji:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <Card title="Analytics" icon="BarChart3">
      View insights and metrics.
    </Card>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Card title="Analytics" icon="BarChart3">
      View insights and metrics.
    </Card>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## CardGroup

A responsive grid layout for organizing multiple Card components.

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <CardGroup cols={2}>
      <Card title="Getting Started" icon="Rocket" href="/introduction">
        Get up and running quickly.
      </Card>
      <Card title="API Reference" icon="Code2" href="/api-reference/overview">
        Explore all available endpoints.
      </Card>
    </CardGroup>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <CardGroup cols={2}>
      <Card title="Getting Started" icon="Rocket" href="/introduction">
        Get up and running quickly.
      </Card>
      <Card title="API Reference" icon="Code2" href="/api-reference/overview">
        Explore all available endpoints.
      </Card>
    </CardGroup>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Props

**Card component**

| Prop       | Type              | Required | Description                                                                   |
| ---------- | ----------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`    | `string`          | yes      | The main heading displayed on the card.                                       |
| `icon`     | `string`          | No       | Name of a Lucide icon (e.g. "Rocket"). Falls back to text/emoji if not found. |
| `href`     | `string`          | No       | If provided, the card becomes clickable and navigates to this route.          |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | No       | Additional descriptive content displayed below the title.                     |

**CardGroup**

| Prop     | Type            | Default | Description                                    |
| -------- | --------------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| cols     | number          | 2       | Number of columns in the grid (1–4 supported). |
| children | React.ReactNode | Yes     | The Card components to render inside the grid. |

## Accessibility Notes

- Cards with `href` behave as links and are keyboard-accessible via Next.js Link.
- Ensure title clearly describes the destination or purpose.
- Avoid relying solely on color to convey meaning.

metadata.title: Cards
metadata.description: Display content in a structured, clickable card layout using Card and CardGroup components.

Page: Expandable


## Overview

The `Expandable` component renders a clickable text trigger that reveals hidden content below it. Unlike `Accordion`, it has no border or card container — it is designed for lightweight inline disclosure within prose, such as optional details, extended explanations, or supplementary examples.

---

## Example

<Expandable title="Show more details">
  This content is hidden by default and revealed when the trigger is clicked.
  Use this for supplementary information that not every reader needs.
</Expandable>

---

## Usage

### Basic expandable

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <Expandable title="Show more details">
      Additional content revealed on click.
    </Expandable>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Expandable title="Show more details">
      Additional content revealed on click.
    </Expandable>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Open by default

Use `defaultOpen` to have the content visible on initial render:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <Expandable title="Implementation notes" defaultOpen>
      This section starts expanded so readers see it immediately.
    </Expandable>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Expandable title="Implementation notes" defaultOpen>
      This section starts expanded so readers see it immediately.
    </Expandable>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### With rich content

Expandable content supports any valid MDX:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
````mdx
    <Expandable title="See the full example">
```ts
      async function fetchUser(id: string) {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error("User not found");
        return res.json();
      }
```

    </Expandable>

`````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Expandable title="See the full example">
````ts
      async function fetchUser(id: string) {
        const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error("User not found");
        return res.json();
      }
`````

    </Expandable>

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Expandable vs Accordion

Both components reveal hidden content, but serve different purposes:

|          | `Expandable`                   | `Accordion`               |
| -------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------- |
| Style    | Minimal, borderless            | Bordered card             |
| Best for | Inline prose, optional details | FAQs, structured sections |
| Grouping | Not supported                  | Use `AccordionGroup`      |

---

## Props

| Prop          | Type              | Required | Default | Description                                       |
| ------------- | ----------------- | -------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`       | `string`          | Yes      | —       | The label shown on the clickable trigger.         |
| `children`    | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | —       | Content revealed when the expandable is open.     |
| `defaultOpen` | `boolean`         | No       | `false` | Whether the content is visible on initial render. |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- The trigger is a `<button>` element and is fully keyboard accessible.
- Use clear, action-oriented titles like "Show full example" or "View type definitions" so users know what to expect before expanding.
- For content that is important for all readers, consider showing it inline rather than hiding it behind an expandable.

metadata.description: A lightweight inline toggle for revealing additional content on demand.

pageContent: Page: Image ## Overview The `DocImage` component renders images with a styled container and optional caption. It also supports theme-aware images — you can provide separate `dark` and `light` sources that swap automatically when the user switches themes. It is also registered as the default `img` renderer, so standard markdown image syntax works out of the box. --- ## Example --- ## Usage ### Standard markdown image Since `DocImage` is registered as the default `img` component, regular markdown syntax is rendered through it automatically: ```mdx ![An example image](/images/hero-dark.png) ``` ![An example image](/images/hero-dark.png) ### With a caption ```mdx ``` ### Theme-aware images Provide separate `dark` and `light` sources to swap images based on the active theme: ```mdx ``` When only one of `dark` or `light` is provided, the other falls back to the base `src`: ```mdx ``` --- ## Props | Prop | Type | Required | Description | | --------- | -------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `src` | `string` | No | Default image source used when no theme-specific source is provided. | | `alt` | `string` | No | Alt text for the image. Defaults to an empty string if omitted. | | `caption` | `string` | No | Optional caption rendered below the image. | | `dark` | `string` | No | Image source used when the dark theme is active. Falls back to `src` if not set. | | `light` | `string` | No | Image source used when the light theme is active. Falls back to `src` if not set. | All standard HTML `` attributes are also accepted and forwarded to the underlying element. --- ## Accessibility Notes - Always provide a meaningful `alt` value describing the image content for screen readers. - Use `caption` to add visible context when the image alone may not be self-explanatory. - Decorative images that convey no information should use `alt=""`.

metadata.description: Display images with optional captions and automatic dark/light mode switching.

Viabl comes with a set of built-in MDX components you can use in any page. No imports needed — they are available globally in every `.mdx` file.

Page: Platform


## Overview

The `Platform` component lets you show different content to users based on their operating system.

Wrap any MDX content—code blocks, notes, images, download buttons, tables, and more—and Viabl automatically shows the correct content for each visitor.
Add a `<PlatformSelector />` anywhere on the page to let users manually switch platforms.

## Basic Usage

````mdx
<PlatformSelector variant="dropdown" />

<Platform on="windows">```powershell winget install myapp ```</Platform>

<Platform on="mac">```bash brew install myapp ```</Platform>

<Platform on="linux">
  ```bash curl -fsSL https://get.myapp.dev | sh ```
</Platform>
````

The visitor's operating system is detected automatically from the browser. A user on macOS sees only the Homebrew command, while the Windows and Linux instructions remain hidden.

---

---

## Supported Platforms

| Platform  | Description                                         |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `windows` | Shown to Windows users.                             |
| `mac`     | Shown to macOS users.                               |
| `linux`   | Shown to Linux users.                               |
| `unknown` | Shown when the operating system cannot be detected. |

---

## PlatformSelector

You can place `<PlatformSelector />`:

- At the top of the page before installation instructions.
- Inline between sections.
- Multiple times on the same page. All selectors stay synchronized.

When they select a platform, every `Platform` block on the page updates simultaneously, and the selected platform persists across pages.

**Usage**

```mdx
<PlatformSelector variant="dropdown" />
```

---

## Targeting Multiple Platforms

Pass an array to `on` when multiple platforms share the same content.

```mdx
<Platform on={["mac", "linux"]}>
  The config file lives at `~/.config/myapp/config.yaml`.
</Platform>

<Platform on="windows">
  The config file lives at `%APPDATA%\myapp\config.yaml`.
</Platform>
```

## Download

The `Download` component automatically renders a platform-aware download button and includes a platform switcher beside it.

```mdx
<Download
  windows="https://github.com/your-org/app/releases/download/v1.0/app.exe"
  mac="https://github.com/your-org/app/releases/download/v1.0/app.dmg"
  linux="https://github.com/your-org/app/releases/download/v1.0/app.AppImage"
  style="block"
  icon="DownloadCloud"
  switcher="dropdown"
/>
```

---

## Props

**Platform**

The `Platform` component accepts the following props.

| Prop | Type                                                  | Description                                                       |
| ---- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `on` | `"windows" \| "mac" \| "linux" \| "unknown"` or array | The platform(s) for which the wrapped content should be rendered. |

**PlatformSelector**

The `PlatformSelector` component accepts the following props.

| Prop        | Type                     | Description                                                                            |
| ----------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `variant`   | `"tabs"` \| `"dropdown"` | Controls the appearance of the selector. Defaults to `"tabs"`.                         |
| `platforms` | `string[]`               | Restricts which platforms appear in the selector. Defaults to all supported platforms. |

**Download**

| Prop       | Description                                                     |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `windows`  | Download URL for Windows users.                                 |
| `mac`      | Download URL for macOS users.                                   |
| `linux`    | Download URL for Linux users.                                   |
| `default`  | Fallback URL used when the platform cannot be detected.         |
| `label`    | Override the button label.                                      |
| `style`    | Button style. Defaults to `"block"`.                            |
| `icon`     | A Lucide icon name.                                             |
| `switcher` | The style of the platform selector displayed beside the button. |

---

metadata.description: Show content conditionally based on the visitor's operating system.

Page: ResponseField


## Overview

The `ResponseField` component renders a single field in an API response schema. Each entry displays the field name, its type, an optional required badge, and a description. Stack multiple `ResponseField` components to document a full response object.

---

## Example

<ResponseField name="id" type="string" required>
  The unique identifier for the resource.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="created_at" type="string">
  ISO 8601 timestamp of when the resource was created.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="metadata" type="object">
  An optional key-value map of additional data attached to the resource.
</ResponseField>

---

## Usage

### Basic field

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <ResponseField name="id" type="string">
      The unique identifier for the resource.
    </ResponseField>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <ResponseField name="id" type="string">
      The unique identifier for the resource.
    </ResponseField>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Required field

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <ResponseField name="email" type="string" required>
      The email address of the user. Must be unique across all accounts.
    </ResponseField>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <ResponseField name="email" type="string" required>
      The email address of the user. Must be unique across all accounts.
    </ResponseField>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Full response object

Stack multiple entries to document a complete response schema:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
        <ResponseField name="id" type="string" required>
        Unique identifier for the user.
        </ResponseField>

        <ResponseField name="name" type="string" required>
        Full display name of the user.
        </ResponseField>

        <ResponseField name="email" type="string" required>
        Email address associated with the account.
        </ResponseField>

        <ResponseField name="role" type="'admin' | 'member' | 'viewer'">
        The user's permission level within the workspace.
        </ResponseField>

        <ResponseField name="created_at" type="string">
        ISO 8601 timestamp of when the account was created.
        </ResponseField>

        <ResponseField name="metadata" type="object">
        Optional key-value pairs of additional data attached to the user.
        </ResponseField>

    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <ResponseField name="id" type="string" required>
      Unique identifier for the user.
    </ResponseField>

    <ResponseField name="name" type="string" required>
      Full display name of the user.
    </ResponseField>

    <ResponseField name="email" type="string" required>
      Email address associated with the account.
    </ResponseField>

    <ResponseField name="role" type="'admin' | 'member' | 'viewer'">
      The user's permission level within the workspace.
    </ResponseField>

    <ResponseField name="created_at" type="string">
      ISO 8601 timestamp of when the account was created.
    </ResponseField>

    <ResponseField name="metadata" type="object">
      Optional key-value pairs of additional data attached to the user.
    </ResponseField>

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Props

| Prop       | Type              | Required | Description                                                     |
| ---------- | ----------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`     | `string`          | Yes      | The field name displayed in monospace.                          |
| `type`     | `string`          | Yes      | The field's type annotation, e.g. `string`, `number`, `object`. |
| `required` | `boolean`         | No       | When present, displays a red `required` badge next to the type. |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | Description of the field and its expected values or behavior.   |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- Field names and types are rendered in `<code>` and monospace text for clarity.
- The `required` badge uses both color and text to convey requirement status — it is not color-only.
- For deeply nested response schemas, consider using `ResponseField` alongside `Expandable` to progressively disclose nested fields.

metadata.description: Document API response fields with name, type, and description in a structured layout.

Page: Steps


## Overview

The `Steps` and `Step` components provide a clean way to present multi-step processes, installation guides, or sequential instructions with numbered indicators and a connecting line.

- **Steps**: The wrapper component that manages numbering and layout.
- **Step**: An individual step with an optional title and content.

---

## Example

<Steps>
  <Step title="Install the package">
    Run the following command in your project root: ````bash npm install
    my-package ````
  </Step>
  <Step title="Configure your environment">
    Add the required environment variables to your `.env` file.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Start the server">
    You're all set. Run `npm run dev` to start your development server.
  </Step>
</Steps>

---

## Usage

### Basic steps

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <Steps>
      <Step title="First step">Content for the first step.</Step>
      <Step title="Second step">Content for the second step.</Step>
    </Steps>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Steps>
      <Step title="First step">Content for the first step.</Step>
      <Step title="Second step">Content for the second step.</Step>
    </Steps>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Steps without titles

The `title` prop is optional. Steps render content-only when omitted:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <Steps>
      <Step>Clone the repository.</Step>
      <Step>Install dependencies with `npm install`.</Step>
      <Step>Run `npm run dev` to start the server.</Step>
    </Steps>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Steps>
      <Step>Clone the repository.</Step>
      <Step>Install dependencies with `npm install`.</Step>
      <Step>Run `npm run dev` to start the server.</Step>
    </Steps>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Steps with rich content

Each step can contain any MDX content including code blocks, callouts, and other components:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ````mdx
    <Steps>
      <Step title="Install dependencies">```bash npm install ```</Step>
      <Step title="Set environment variables">
        <Note>Copy `.env.example` to `.env` before editing.</Note>
        Add your API keys to the `.env` file.
      </Step>
    </Steps>
    ````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Steps>
      <Step title="Install dependencies">````bash npm install ````</Step>
      <Step title="Set environment variables">
        <Note>Copy `.env.example` to `.env` before editing.</Note>
        Add your API keys to the `.env` file.
      </Step>
    </Steps>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Props

**Steps**

| Prop       | Type              | Required | Description                              |
| ---------- | ----------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | One or more `Step` components to render. |

**Step**

| Prop       | Type              | Required | Description                                                          |
| ---------- | ----------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`    | `string`          | No       | Heading displayed next to the step number.                           |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | The content of the step. Accepts any valid MDX including components. |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- Steps are purely visual and rendered as `div` elements — they do not use `ol`/`li` semantics. If strict list semantics matter, consider supplementing with screen-reader-only text.
- Ensure each step title clearly describes the action to be taken.
- Avoid skipping logical sequence — steps are numbered automatically starting from 1.

Page: Tooltip


## Overview

The `Tooltip` component renders a small floating label when the user hovers over its content. It is ideal for defining terms, clarifying abbreviations, or adding supplementary information without cluttering the page.

---

## Example

Hover over <Tooltip tip="This is the tooltip content">this text</Tooltip> to see the tooltip.

---

## Usage

### Basic tooltip

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <Tooltip tip="A reusable unit of UI">component</Tooltip>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Tooltip tip="A reusable unit of UI">component</Tooltip>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Inline with prose

Tooltips sit naturally within sentences:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">

    ```mdx
    Pass your{" "}
    <Tooltip tip="JSON Web Token used for authentication">JWT</Tooltip> in the
    `Authorization` header of every request.
    ```

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    Pass your{" "}
    <Tooltip tip="JSON Web Token used for authentication">JWT</Tooltip> in the
    `Authorization` header of every request.`
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Props

| Prop       | Type              | Required | Description                                            |
| ---------- | ----------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `tip`      | `string`          | Yes      | The text displayed inside the floating tooltip label.  |
| `children` | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | The inline content that triggers the tooltip on hover. |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- The trigger element uses a dashed underline and `cursor-help` to signal to users that additional information is available.
- Tooltips are currently mouse-only and not accessible via keyboard or touch. For critical information, consider including it inline rather than hiding it in a tooltip.
- Avoid putting interactive elements or long passages inside `tip` — keep tooltip text brief and descriptive.

Page: Update


## Overview

The `Update` component renders a single entry in a vertical timeline. Each entry has a labeled marker, an optional description, and freeform content. Stack multiple `Update` components to build a changelog or release history page.

---

## Example

<Update label="v1.2.0" description="January 2025">
  Added dark mode support and improved mobile responsiveness across all
  components.
</Update>

<Update label="v1.1.0" description="December 2024">
  Introduced the `Expandable` and `Tooltip` components.
</Update>

<Update label="v1.0.0" description="November 2024">
  Initial release with core component set.
</Update>

---

## Usage

### Basic update entry

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <Update label="v1.0.0" description="November 2024">
      Initial release with core component set.
    </Update>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Update label="v1.0.0" description="November 2024">
      Initial release with core component set.
    </Update>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Without description

The `description` prop is optional — the label stands alone when omitted:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
    ```mdx
    <Update label="Hotfix">
      Fixed a critical issue with token validation on the `/auth/refresh`
      endpoint.
    </Update>
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Update label="Hotfix">
      Fixed a critical issue with token validation on the `/auth/refresh`
      endpoint.
    </Update>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### Changelog page

Stack multiple entries to build a full changelog:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
```mdx
    <Update label="v2.0.0" description="March 2025">
      Major release. Redesigned the config system and added OpenAPI support.
    </Update>

    <Update label="v1.3.0" description="February 2025">
      Added the `Update`, `Badge`, and `Tooltip` components.
    </Update>

    <Update label="v1.0.0" description="November 2024">
      Initial release.
    </Update>

````
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Update label="v2.0.0" description="March 2025">
      Major release. Redesigned the config system and added OpenAPI support.
    </Update>

    <Update label="v1.3.0" description="February 2025">
      Added the `Update`, `Badge`, and `Tooltip` components.
    </Update>

    <Update label="v1.0.0" description="November 2024">
      Initial release.
    </Update>
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

### With rich content

Each entry supports any valid MDX content:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Code">
```mdx
    <Update label="v1.2.0" description="January 2025">
      **Breaking changes:**
      - Renamed `DocImage` prop `darkSrc` to `dark`
      - Removed deprecated `size` prop from `Badge`

      **New features:**
      - Added `defaultOpen` prop to `Expandable`
      - Introduced `AccordionGroup` wrapper component
    </Update>
````

  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Output">
    <Update label="v1.2.0" description="January 2025">
      **Breaking changes:**
      - Renamed `DocImage` prop `darkSrc` to `dark`
      - Removed deprecated `size` prop from `Badge`

      **New features:**
      - Added `defaultOpen` prop to `Expandable`
      - Introduced `AccordionGroup` wrapper component
    </Update>

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

---

## Props

| Prop          | Type              | Required | Description                                                         |
| ------------- | ----------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `label`       | `string`          | Yes      | The version, date, or tag shown in the accent-colored marker badge. |
| `description` | `string`          | No       | Secondary text shown beside the label, typically a date or summary. |
| `children`    | `React.ReactNode` | Yes      | The content of the update entry. Accepts any valid MDX.             |

---

## Accessibility Notes

- The timeline is rendered using `div` elements with no semantic list markup. If strict chronological semantics matter, consider wrapping entries in an `<ol>` via a custom layout.
- Use consistent `label` formatting across entries — either always use version numbers or always use dates — to help readers scan the timeline quickly.

Page: Docker


Docker is the most portable way to deploy Viabl. Build once, run anywhere — on a VPS, a Kubernetes cluster, or any container hosting platform.

## Prerequisites

<Check>Docker installed on your machine</Check>
<Check>Docker installed on your target server</Check>
<Check>`viabl build` run successfully — `.viabl/` folder exists</Check>

## Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` at the root of your docs project:

```dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Copy the build output
COPY .viabl/ .

EXPOSE 7777

CMD ["node", "start.js"]
```

<Note>
  The `Dockerfile` lives at your project root alongside `docs.json`, not inside
  `.viabl/`. The build context is your project root and we copy only the
  `.viabl/` folder into the image.
</Note>

## Build the image

```bash
docker build -t my-docs .
```

Replace `my-docs` with whatever name makes sense for your project.

## Run the container

```bash
docker run -d \
  --name my-docs \
  -p 7777:7777 \
  -e PORT=7777 \
  my-docs
```

Your docs are now live at `http://localhost:7777`.

<ResponseField name="-d" type="flag">
  Run the container in detached mode — it keeps running after you close the
  terminal.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="--name" type="string">
  A name for the container so you can reference it easily with `docker stop`,
  `docker logs` etc.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="-p 7777:7777" type="string">
  Maps port `7777` on the host to port `7777` inside the container. Change the
  left side to use a different host port.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="-e PORT=7777" type="string">
  Sets the `PORT` environment variable inside the container. Must match the
  right side of `-p`.
</ResponseField>

## Useful commands

```bash
# View logs
docker logs my-docs

# Follow logs in real time
docker logs -f my-docs

# Stop the container
docker stop my-docs

# Restart the container
docker restart my-docs

# Remove the container
docker rm -f my-docs
```

## Updating your docs

When you make changes to your docs:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Rebuild">
    Run `viabl build` in your docs project to regenerate `.viabl/`.

```bash
    viabl build
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Rebuild the image">
    
```bash
    docker build -t my-docs .
```
    
  </Step>
  <Step title="Replace the running container">
    
```bash
    docker rm -f my-docs
    docker run -d --name my-docs -p 7777:7777 -e PORT=7777 my-docs
```
   
  </Step>
</Steps>

## Running multiple projects

Run each project as a separate container on a different port:

```bash
# Project 1
docker run -d --name docs-project-1 -p 7777:7777 -e PORT=7777 project-1-image

# Project 2
docker run -d --name docs-project-2 -p 8777:8777 -e PORT=8777 project-2-image
```

## Docker Compose

For a more manageable setup, use Docker Compose. Create a `docker-compose.yml` at your project root:

```yaml
services:
  docs:
    build: .
    container_name: my-docs
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "7777:7777"
    environment:
      PORT: 7777
```

Then start it with:

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

And update it with:

```bash
viabl build
docker compose up -d --build
```

<Tip>
  `restart: unless-stopped` ensures your docs container restarts automatically
  if the server reboots or the process crashes.
</Tip>

## Using a reverse proxy

In production you will typically put a reverse proxy like Nginx or Caddy in front of your container to handle HTTPS and custom domains.

With Caddy this is as simple as:

```
your-docs.example.com {
  reverse_proxy localhost:7777
}
```

Caddy handles SSL certificates automatically via Let's Encrypt. See the [VPS guide](/deployment/vps) for a full Nginx setup.

metadata.description: Build a Docker image and run your Viabl docs in a container.

Page: GitHub Actions


GitHub Actions lets you automatically build and deploy your docs every time you push changes to your repository. No manual builds, no manual deploys.

## How it works

```
git push → GitHub Actions triggers → viabl build → deploy to your server
```

The workflow installs the Viabl CLI, runs `viabl build`, then copies the `.viabl/` folder to your server and restarts the running process.

## Prerequisites

<Check>Your docs project is in a GitHub repository</Check>
<Check>A server with Node.js 20+ and SSH access</Check>
<Check>
  SSH key pair — private key stored as a GitHub secret, public key on your
  server
</Check>
<Check>
  `viabl` installed on the server or installed as part of the workflow
</Check>

## Setting up secrets

Go to your GitHub repository → **Settings** → **Secrets and variables** → **Actions** and add the following secrets:

<ResponseField name="SSH_HOST" type="secret">
  The IP address or hostname of your server.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="SSH_USER" type="secret">
  The SSH username to connect with. Example: `ubuntu`, `root`, `deploy`.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" type="secret">
  The private SSH key used to connect to your server. Paste the full contents of
  your `.pem` or private key file.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="SSH_PORT" type="secret">
  The SSH port on your server. Usually `22`.
</ResponseField>

## Basic workflow

Create `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` in your docs repository:

```yaml
name: Deploy Docs

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout

pageContent:
## With Docker

If you are deploying with Docker, replace the copy and restart steps with a Docker build and run:

```yaml
name: Deploy Docs

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20

      - name: Install Viabl CLI
        run: npm install -g @viablkit/cli
      - name: Build docs
        run: viabl build

      - name: Copy build to server
        uses: appleboy/scp-action@v0.1.7
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.VPS_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.VPS_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.VPS_SSH_KEY }}
          source: ".viabl/,Dockerfile"
          target: "/srv/my-docs"
          rm: true

      - name: Build and restart Docker container
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1.0.3
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.VPS_HOST }}
          username: ${{ secrets.VPS_USER }}
          key: ${{ secrets.VPS_SSH_KEY }}
          script: |
            cd /srv/my-docs
            docker build --no-cache -t my-docs.
            docker rm -f my-docs|| true
            docker run -d \
            --name my-docs\
            --restart unless-stopped \
            -p 7777:7777 \
            -e PORT=7777 \
            viabl-docs
            docker image prune -f
```

## With Railway

If you are deploying to Railway, use the Railway CLI in your workflow instead:

```yaml
- name: Install Railway CLI
  run: npm install -g @railway/cli

- name: Deploy to Railway
  run: railway up --service my-docs
  env:
    RAILWAY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.RAILWAY_TOKEN }}
```

Add `RAILWAY_TOKEN` as a GitHub secret — get it from your Railway account settings.

## Caching the Viabl CLI

On every run the workflow installs the CLI from scratch. Speed this up by caching the global npm prefix:

```yaml
- name: Cache Viabl CLI
  uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm-global
    key: viabl-cli-${{ runner.os }}

- name: Install Viabl CLI
  run: |
    npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global
    npm install -g @viablkit/cli
    echo "$HOME/.npm-global/bin" >> $GITHUB_PATH
```

## Only deploy on changes to docs

If your docs repo also contains other code, trigger the workflow only when docs files change:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    paths:
      - "**.mdx"
      - "**.md"
      - "docs.json"
      - "public/**"
      - "openapi.yaml"
```

pageContent:
Page: Deployment Overview


Viabl is self-hosted — you own the infrastructure and decide where your docs run. The `viabl build` command packages everything into a single self-contained folder you can deploy anywhere that runs Node.js.

## How it works

<Steps>
  <Step title="Build">
    Run `viabl build` inside your docs project. This downloads the exact renderer and content server versions and packages them together with your docs into a `.viabl/` folder.

```bash
    viabl build
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Copy to your server">
    Copy the `.viabl/` folder to your server, Docker image, or CI artifact. It is completely self-contained — no internet connection needed at runtime.
  </Step>
  <Step title="Run">
    Start the server with a `PORT` environment variable.

```bash
    PORT=7777 node .viabl/start.js
```

    Your docs are live at the port you specified.

  </Step>
</Steps>

## What viabl build produces

After running `viabl build` your project will have a `.viabl/` folder:

```
.viabl/
├── renderer/          ← Next.js standalone build
├── content-server/    ← Express content server
│   └── dist/
│       └── index.js
├── docs/              ← your docs files, copied in
│   ├── docs.json
│   ├── introduction.mdx
│   └── ...
└── start.js           ← single entry point that boots everything
```

<Note>
  Add `.viabl/` to your `.gitignore` — it is a build artifact and should not be
  committed to git.
</Note>

## The start.js entry point

`start.js` is the only file you need to run. It boots both the renderer and content server as separate processes and manages their lifecycle.

<ResponseField name="PORT" type="number" required>
  The port your docs will be served on. There is no default — you must provide
  this.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="CONTENT_PORT" type="number">
  The port the internal content server runs on. Defaults to `PORT + 1`. You only
  need to set this if you are running multiple docs projects on the same server
  and need to avoid port conflicts.
</ResponseField>
```bash # Basic usage PORT=7777 node .viabl/start.js

# With explicit content port

PORT=7777 CONTENT_PORT=8777 node .viabl/start.js

````

## Running multiple projects

Each docs project is completely independent. Run them on different ports:
```bash
# Project 1
PORT=7777 node /srv/docs-project-1/.viabl/start.js

# Project 2
PORT=8777 node /srv/docs-project-2/.viabl/start.js
````

<Warning>
  Never run two projects on the same `PORT`. Each project also needs a unique
  `CONTENT_PORT` — if you do not set it explicitly it defaults to `PORT + 1`, so
  two projects on ports `7777` and `7778` would conflict on the content port.
  Use ports that are at least 2 apart, or set `CONTENT_PORT` explicitly.
</Warning>

## Requirements

<Check>Node.js 20 or higher on the target server</Check>
<Check>Ports open in your firewall for the ports you choose</Check>
<Check>A process manager like PM2 or systemd to keep the server running</Check>

## Deployment guides

    Build a Docker image and run your docs in a container.
  </Card>
  <Card title="GitHub Actions" icon="GitBranch" href="/guides/github-actions">
    Automate your docs deployment with a GitHub Actions workflow.
  </Card>

    title="Hosting Under a Subpath"
    icon="Server"
    href="/guides/host-under-subpath"
  >
    How to host your Viabl docs under a subpath like /docs on your main domain.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

pageContent:
Page: AI Assistant


Viabl supports adding an AI assistant directly to your documentation. Users can ask questions and get answers grounded in your docs content. You can use any of the supported providers — Anthropic, OpenAI, or a self-hosted Ollama instance.

## Configuration

Add an `ai` field to your `docs.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://viabl.dev/schema/docs.json",
  "name": "My Docs",
  "ai": {
    "provider": "anthropic",
    "apiKey": "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}",
    "suggestedQuestions": [
      "How do I get started?",
      "What are the system requirements?"
    ],
    "rules": [
      "Always respond in a friendly and concise tone.",
      "Do not answer questions unrelated to this documentation."
    ]
  },
  "navigation": []
}
```

<Note>
  All fields under `ai` support environment variable interpolation using `$
  {VAR_NAME}` syntax. This keeps sensitive values like API keys out of your
  committed `docs.json`.
</Note>

## Providers

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Anthropic">
```json
    "ai": {
      "provider": "anthropic",
      "apiKey": "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}",
      "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5",
      "suggestedQuestions": [
        "How do I install the CLI?",
        "How do I deploy my docs?"
      ]
    }
```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="OpenAI">
```json
    "ai": {
      "provider": "openai",
      "apiKey": "${OPENAI_API_KEY}",
      "model": "gpt-4o",
      "embeddingModel": "text-embedding-3-small",
      "suggestedQuestions": [
        "What components are available?",
        "How do I configure navigation?"
      ]
    }
```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Ollama">
```json
    "ai": {
      "provider": "ollama",
      "endpoint": "http://localhost:11434",
      "model": "llama3",
      "embeddingModel": "nomic-embed-text",
      "suggestedQuestions": [
        "How do I get started?"
      ]
    }
```

    <Note>
      `endpoint` is required for Ollama and should point to where your Ollama instance is running. No API key is needed.
    </Note>

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Fields reference

<ResponseField
  name="provider"
  type='"anthropic" | "openai" | "ollama"'
  required
>
  The AI provider to use.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="apiKey" type="string">
  Your API key for the provider. Supports environment variable interpolation —
  use `${YOUR_ENV_VAR}` to keep keys out of your repo. Not required for Ollama.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="endpoint" type="string">
  The URL where your Ollama instance is running. Required for Ollama, ignored for other providers.

```json
  "endpoint": "http://localhost:11434"
```

</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="model" type="string">
  The model to use for generating responses. If not set, the provider default is
  used.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="embeddingModel" type="string">
  The model to use for generating embeddings when indexing your docs content. If
  not set, the provider default is used.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="suggestedQuestions" type="string[]">
  A list of starter questions shown to users when they first open the assistant. Helps users understand what they can ask.

```json
  "suggestedQuestions": [
    "How do I install the CLI?",
    "What MDX components are available?",
    "How do I deploy my docs?"
  ]
```

</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="rules" type="string[]">
  Instructions the AI strictly follows when responding. Use this to constrain tone, scope, or behavior.

```json
  "rules": [
    "Only answer questions related to this documentation.",
    "Always suggest the user check the relevant docs page.",
    "Respond in English only."
  ]
```

</ResponseField>

## Environment variables

All fields under `ai` accept environment variable references using `${VAR_NAME}` syntax. This applies to `apiKey`, `endpoint`, `model`, `embeddingModel`, and even individual entries inside `suggestedQuestions` and `rules`.

Create a `.env` file at your project root:

```bash
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
```

Then reference it in `docs.json`:

```json
"ai": {
  "provider": "anthropic",
  "apiKey": "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"
}
```

<Warning>
  Never commit API keys directly to your `docs.json`. Always use environment
  variable references and add your `.env` file to `.gitignore`.
</Warning>

Page: Configuration


All configuration for your Viabl project lives in a single `docs.json` file at the root of your project. Add the `$schema` field to get full intellisense and validation in VS Code.

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://viabl.dev/schema/docs.json",
  "name": "My Docs",
  "navigation": [
    {
      "group": "Getting Started",
      "pages": ["introduction"]
    }
  ]
}
```

<Note>
  Only `name` and `navigation` are required. Everything else is optional.
</Note>

## Identity

<ResponseField name="name" type="string" required>
  The name of your documentation site. Shown in the browser tab and header.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="favicon" type="string">
  Path to your favicon relative to the project root.
```json
  { "favicon": "/favicon.png" }
```
</ResponseField>

## Logo

Controls the logo shown in the top left of your docs.

<ResponseField name="logo.light" type="string">
  Path to the logo image used in light mode.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="logo.dark" type="string">
  Path to the logo image used in dark mode.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="logo.href" type="string">
  URL to navigate to when the logo is clicked. Defaults to the docs root.
</ResponseField>
```json
"logo": {
  "light": "/logo/light.svg",
  "dark": "/logo/dark.svg",
  "href": "https://example.com"
}
```

## Colors

Brand color configuration. Controls the accent colors used throughout your docs.

<ResponseField name="colors.primary" type="string">
  Base brand color used as the default accent. Example: `#ff5800`
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="colors.light" type="string">
  Color variant for light backgrounds — usually darker or more saturated for
  contrast on white.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="colors.dark" type="string">
  Color variant for dark backgrounds — usually lighter or more vibrant to pop on
  dark.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="colors.background.light" type="string">
  Background color for light mode. Supports CSS gradients.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="colors.background.dark" type="string">
  Background color for dark mode. Supports CSS gradients.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="colors.anchors.from" type="string">
  Start color of the anchor icon gradient in the sidebar.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="colors.anchors.to" type="string">
  End color of the anchor icon gradient in the sidebar.
</ResponseField>
```json
"colors": {
  "primary": "#ff5800",
  "light": "#ff5800",
  "dark": "#ff7733",
  "background": {
    "dark": "radial-gradient(ellipse 80% 50% at 50% -20%, rgba(255,88,0,0.15), transparent), #0c0d0f",
    "light": "#ffffff"
  },
  "anchors": {
    "from": "#ff5800",
    "to": "#ce0569"
  }
}
```

pageContent:
## Fonts

Custom font configuration for headings and body text.

<ResponseField name="font.headings.family" type="string">
  Font family name for headings. Example: `Inter`
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="font.headings.url" type="string">
  URL to load the heading font from. Example: a Google Fonts CSS URL.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="font.body.family" type="string">
  Font family name for body text.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="font.body.url" type="string">
  URL to load the body font from.
</ResponseField>
```json
"font": {
  "headings": {
    "family": "Geist",
    "url": "https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Geist"
  },
  "body": {
    "family": "Geist",
    "url": "https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Geist"
  }
}
```

## Navigation

The sidebar navigation structure. Viabl supports three navigation formats — a simple array of groups, a dictionary mapped to tabs, and raw strings for headerless sidebar items.

<ResponseField
  name="navigation"
  type="NavigationGroup[] | Record<string, NavigationGroup[]>"
  required
>
  The sidebar navigation structure. Accepts a flat array of groups for simple
  sites, or a dictionary object mapping tab URLs to navigation arrays for tabbed
  sites.
</ResponseField>

```json
"navigation": [
  {
    "group": "Getting Started",
    "icon": "BookOpen",
    "pages": ["introduction", "getting-started"]
  }
]
```

See the [Navigation](/docs/quickstart/navigation) page for all supported formats including dictionary navigation, persistent sidebar items, and raw string pages.

## Top Bar

### Links

<ResponseField name="topbarLinks[].name" type="string" required>
  Display text for the link.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="topbarLinks[].url" type="string" required>
  URL the link points to.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="topbarLinks[].blank" type="boolean">
  Whether the link opens in a new tab. Defaults to `false`.
</ResponseField>
```json
"topbarLinks": [
  { "name": "Support", "url": "https://example.com/support", "blank": true }
]
```

### CTA Button

<ResponseField name="topbarCtaButton.name" type="string" required>
  Button label text.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="topbarCtaButton.url" type="string" required>
  URL the button links to.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="topbarCtaButton.style" type='"fill" | "outline"'>
  Visual style of the button. Defaults to `fill`.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="topbarCtaButton.arrow" type="boolean">
  Whether to show an arrow icon next to the label. Defaults to `false`.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="topbarCtaButton.icon" type="string">
  Icon name to show inside the button.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="topbarCtaButton.anchor" type="boolean">
  Pin the button to the right side of the top bar.
</ResponseField>
```json
"topbarCtaButton": {
  "name": "Get Started",
  "url": "https://example.com/signup",
  "style": "fill",
  "arrow": true
}
```

pageContent:
## Tabs

Tabs shown below the top navigation bar for switching between major sections.

<ResponseField name="tabs[].name" type="string" required>
  Tab label text.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="tabs[].url" type="string" required>
  URL default path that should be open by default when we open the tab.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="tabs[].icon" type="string">
  Icon name shown next to the tab label.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="tabs[].anchor" type="boolean">
  Pin this tab to the right side of the tab bar.
</ResponseField>
```json
"tabs": [
  { "name": "Documentation", "url": "docs", "icon": "BookOpen" },
  { "name": "API Reference", "url": "api-reference", "icon": "Code2" }
  {"name": "Feedback", "url": "feedback", "icon": "Code2", "anchor": true }
]
```

## Anchors

Special links shown at the top of the sidebar before navigation groups. Good for GitHub, Discord, or any external link you want to surface prominently.

<ResponseField name="anchors[].name" type="string" required>
  Display name of the anchor link.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="anchors[].url" type="string" required>
  URL the anchor links to.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="anchors[].icon" type="string">
  Icon name shown next to the anchor.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="anchors[].color" type="string">
  Custom color for the anchor icon.
</ResponseField>
```json
"anchors": [
  {
    "name": "GitHub",
    "icon": "Github",
    "url": "https://github.com/your-org/your-repo",
    "color": "#333333"
  },
  {
    "name": "Discord",
    "icon": "MessageCircle",
    "url": "https://discord.gg/your-invite",
    "color": "#5865f2"
  }
]
```

## Versions

Show a version switcher in the top bar to let users switch between different versions of your docs.

<ResponseField name="versions" type="string[]">
  List of version identifiers. Each version should have a corresponding folder
  at the project root.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="defaultVersion" type="string">
  The version shown by default. Must match one of the values in `versions`.
</ResponseField>
```json "versions": ["v1", "v2"], "defaultVersion": "v2" ```

<Tip>
  Each version folder should mirror your root docs structure. For example
  `v2/introduction.mdx` serves the introduction page for version `v2`.
</Tip>

pageContent:
## Footer Socials

Social media links shown in the footer.

<ResponseField name="footerSocials.x" type="string">X (Twitter) profile URL.</ResponseField>
<ResponseField name="footerSocials.github" type="string">GitHub profile or organization URL.</ResponseField>
<ResponseField name="footerSocials.linkedin" type="string">LinkedIn profile or company URL.</ResponseField>
<ResponseField name="footerSocials.discord" type="string">Discord invite URL.</ResponseField>
<ResponseField name="footerSocials.youtube" type="string">YouTube channel URL.</ResponseField>
<ResponseField name="footerSocials.website" type="string">Your main website URL.</ResponseField>
```json
"footerSocials": {
  "github": "https://github.com/your-org",
  "x": "https://x.com/your-handle",
  "discord": "https://discord.gg/your-invite"
}
```

## SEO

<ResponseField name="seo.indexHiding" type="boolean">
  Set to `true` to prevent search engines from indexing your entire docs site.
  Defaults to `false`. To hide individual pages only, use `noIndex` in page
  frontmatter.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="seo.og.title" type="string">
  Title shown in social media previews.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="seo.og.description" type="string">
  Description shown in social media previews.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="seo.og.image" type="string">
  Path to the Open Graph image. Recommended size is `1200 × 630px`.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="aiScraping" type="boolean">
  Whether to allow known AI crawlers to index your docs. Defaults to `true`. Set
  to `false` to block AI bots via the generated `robots.txt`.
</ResponseField>

```json
"aiScraping": false,
"seo": {
  "indexHiding": false,
  "og": {
    "title": "My Docs",
    "description": "Documentation for My Product",
    "image": "/og-image.png"
  }
}
```

Viabl also generates a sitemap, `robots.txt`, and `llms.txt` automatically. See the [SEO & Discoverability](/docs/quickstart/seo) page for the full reference.

</ResponseField>
```json
"search": {
  "prompt": "Search the docs..."
}
```

Page: Writing Pages


Pages in Viabl are MDX files — Markdown with the ability to use React components inline. Every page lives in your project root and is registered in `docs.json` by its slug.

## Creating a page

Create an MDX file anywhere in your project root:

```
my-docs/
├── docs.json
├── introduction.mdx        ← slug: "introduction"
├── getting-started.mdx     ← slug: "getting-started"
└── guides/
    └── deployment.mdx      ← slug: "guides/deployment"
```

Then register it in `docs.json`:

```json
"navigation": [
  {
    "group": "Getting Started",
    "pages": ["introduction", "getting-started"]
  },
  {
    "group": "Guides",
    "pages": ["guides/deployment"]
  }
]
```

<Note>
  Page slugs are relative to the project root and have no file extension. A file
  at `guides/deployment.mdx` has the slug `guides/deployment`.
</Note>

## Frontmatter

Every page should start with a frontmatter block — a YAML section between `---` delimiters. It controls the page title, description, and other metadata.

```mdx
---
title: Getting Started
description: Get up and running with Viabl in minutes.
icon: Rocket
---

Your page content starts here.
```

<ResponseField name="title" type="string" required>
  The page title. Shown in the browser tab, sidebar, and at the top of the page.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="description" type="string">
  A short description of the page. Shown below the title and used for SEO.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="icon" type="string">
  A Lucide icon name shown next to the page title. Example: `Rocket`, `Code2`,
  `Settings`.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="openapi" type="string">
  Path to an OpenAPI spec file. When set, the page renders as an API reference
  page.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="openapiTag" type="string">
  Filter the OpenAPI spec to only show endpoints matching this tag.
</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="noIndex" type="boolean">
  Hide this specific page from search engine indexing. Useful when `seo.indexHiding` is `false` globally but you want certain pages excluded — internal guides, draft pages, or anything not meant for public search results.

```mdx
---
title: Internal Guide
noIndex: true
---
```

</ResponseField>

<ResponseField name="ogImage" type="string">
  A custom Open Graph image for this specific page. Used when the page is shared on social media — overrides the global `seo.og.image` set in `docs.json`.

```mdx
---
title: Getting Started
ogImage: /images/og-getting-started.png
---
```

Place the image in folders named `images`, `assets` or `media`. Recommended size is `1200 × 630px`.

</ResponseField>

## Writing content

Pages support the full Markdown syntax plus all Viabl components.

### Headings

```mdx

pageContent:
## Writing content

Pages support the full Markdown syntax plus all Viabl components.

### Headings

```mdx
## Section heading

### Subsection heading

#### Smaller heading
```

Headings are automatically added to the table of contents on the right side of the page.

### Text formatting

```mdx
**Bold text**
_Italic text_
~~Strikethrough~~
`inline code`
```

### Links

```mdx
[External link](https://example.com)
[Internal link](/getting-started)
```

### Lists

```mdx
- Unordered item
- Another item
  - Nested item

1. First step
2. Second step
3. Third step
```

### Images

```mdx
![Alt text](/images/my-image.png)
```

Place image files in your project root — a common convention is an `images/` folder. Reference them with an absolute path from the project root.

### Code blocks

Fenced code blocks with a language identifier get full syntax highlighting:

````mdx
```typescript
const response = await fetch("/api/users");
const data = await response.json();
```
````

Add a filename after the language to show a title bar:

````mdx
```typescript index.ts
const response = await fetch("/api/users");
```
````

### Tables

```mdx
| Name  | Type   | Description        |
| ----- | ------ | ------------------ |
| id    | string | Unique identifier  |
| email | string | User email address |
| role  | string | User role          |
```

## Organizing pages

### Nested groups

Navigation groups can be nested to create sub-sections in the sidebar:

```json
"navigation": [
  {
    "group": "Guides",
    "pages": [
      "guides/overview",
      {
        "group": "Advanced",
        "pages": [
          "guides/advanced/custom-domain",
          "guides/advanced/versioning"
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

### Group icons

Add an icon to any navigation group:

```json
{
  "group": "Getting Started",
  "icon": "BookOpen",
  "pages": ["introduction", "getting-started"]
}
```

<Tip>
  Icons use Lucide icon names. Browse all available icons at
  [lucide.dev](https://lucide.dev).
</Tip>

## Versioned pages

If your docs have multiple versions, create a folder for each version at the project root:

```
my-docs/
├── docs.json
├── introduction.mdx         ← shared across all versions
└── v2/
    └── introduction.mdx     ← overrides for v2
```

Configure versions in `docs.json`:

```json
"versions": ["v1", "v2"],
"defaultVersion": "v2"
```

When a user selects a version, Viabl looks for the page in the version folder first, then falls back to the root.

## API reference pages

To create an API reference page from an OpenAPI spec, point to your spec file in the frontmatter:

```mdx
---
title: API Reference
openapi: /openapi.yaml
---
```

To filter the spec to a specific tag:

```mdx
---
title: Users API
openapi: /openapi.yaml
openapiTag: Users
---
```

Place your OpenAPI spec file at the project root. Both `.yaml` and `.json` formats are supported.

<Warning>
  The `openapi` frontmatter field replaces the page body entirely. Any MDX
  content below the frontmatter will be ignored when `openapi` is set.
</Warning>

## Live reload

While running `viabl dev`, any change to an MDX file or `docs.json` is reflected in the browser automatically — no manual refresh needed.

<Check>Edit page content — reloads instantly</Check>
<Check>Add a new page to navigation — sidebar updates</Check>
<Check>Change frontmatter title — tab title and heading update</Check>
<Check>Add or remove a navigation group — sidebar updates</Check>

## installation

<Steps>
  <Step title="Install the CLI">
    Install the Viabl CLI globally with npm.

```bash
    npm install -g @viablkit/cli
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Create your project">
    Scaffold a new docs project from the starter template.

```bash
    viabl init my-docs
    cd my-docs
```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Start writing">
    Start the local dev server and open your browser.

```bash
    viabl dev
```

    Your docs are live at `http://localhost:7777`. Edit any MDX file and the browser reloads automatically.

  </Step>
</Steps>

## Core concepts

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="docs.json — your single config file" defaultOpen>
    Everything about your docs lives in one file — navigation structure, branding, colors, fonts, versioning, and more. No scattered config files, no complex setup.

      "navigation": [
        {
          "group": "Getting Started",
          "pages": ["introduction", "getting-started"]
        }

```

  <Accordion title="MDX — write with superpowers">

  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Self-hosted — deploy anywhere">
    Viabl runs on your own infrastructure. Build a production bundle with `viabl build` and deploy it to any VPS, Docker container, or hosting platform that runs Node.js.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
